# BankSight — What We Found (Plain-Language Summary)

This document explains, in everyday language, what the banking data analysis actually
showed. No code, no SQL — just the findings and why they matter.

---

## The Dataset in Plain Terms

We looked at a made-up (synthetic) bank's data:
- 50,000 customers
- 75,000 bank accounts (checking, savings, business)
- 100,000 debit/credit cards
- 30,000 loans
- 1,000,000 transactions (purchases/payments) from 2019 to 2025

"Synthetic" means this data was generated by a computer to *look* like real banking
data, rather than coming from an actual bank. That distinction matters a lot for the
findings below.

---

## Finding 1: The data itself is very clean

**What we checked:** Are there any missing values, duplicate records, or broken links
between tables (e.g. a transaction that points to an account that doesn't exist)?

**What we found:** Nothing wrong at all. Every table is complete, nothing is duplicated,
and every record correctly links to where it should.

**Why it matters:** In the real world, data is almost never this clean — you'd normally
spend a lot of time fixing messy data before you could even start analyzing it. This
tells us the dataset was artificially generated to be "textbook perfect," which is
useful for practicing analysis skills, but real bank data would need much more cleanup.

---

## Finding 2: Account type doesn't really matter here

**What we checked:** Do checking, savings, and business accounts hold different amounts
of money on average?

**What we found:** No — all three account types hold almost exactly the same total
amount of money (about $2.5 billion each).

**Why it matters:** In a real bank, you'd expect these to look quite different (e.g.
business accounts usually hold more money than personal checking accounts). Here, they
don't, which is another sign the data was randomly generated rather than modeled on real
banking behavior.

---

## Finding 3: Credit score doesn't affect loan interest rate (but it should)

**What we checked:** Do customers with worse credit scores get charged higher interest
rates on their loans? This is one of the most basic rules in real-world lending.

**What we found:** No meaningful difference at all. Whether someone's credit score is
"Poor" or "Excellent," their average interest rate is basically the same (around
8.5% either way).

**Why it matters:** This is the single most important finding in the whole project. In
real banking, this relationship is one of the strongest and most expected patterns in
the data — poor credit almost always means a higher interest rate. Finding that it's
*not* true here tells us interest rates in this dataset were assigned randomly, not
based on customer risk. **This is a good thing to point out in an interview** — it shows
you know how to check whether a dataset behaves the way real-world data should, instead
of just assuming it does.

---

## Finding 4: Customer segmentation — grouping customers by risk

**What we did:** We grouped all 50,000 customers into four categories based on their
credit score and how much debt they carry relative to their savings:

| Segment | What it means | How many customers |
|---|---|---|
| Premium | Good credit, low debt — banks want to keep these customers happy | ~7,400 |
| Standard | Decent credit, manageable debt | ~7,000 |
| High Debt Burden | Owes more than they have saved — worth monitoring | ~6,400 |
| Subprime | Lower credit score, higher risk | ~29,200 |

**Why it matters:** This kind of grouping is exactly what banks use in real life to
decide who gets premium offers, who needs a check-in call, etc. However, because
(as we saw in Finding 1) credit scores here are spread evenly from bad to excellent
instead of clustering around "decent" like in real life, way more customers ended up
in the "Subprime" bucket than a real bank would ever see. **The method we used is
correct and reusable — it's the input data that's unrealistic, not the approach.**

---

## Finding 5: Looking for unusual/suspicious transactions

**What we did:** We tried to flag transactions that looked unusually large — a basic
first step in fraud detection.

**What we found:** Every transaction amount falls somewhere between $1 and $10,000,
and they're spread out *evenly* across that whole range — not clustered around a
typical amount with occasional larger ones (which is how real spending behaves). Because
of this, there's no such thing as a truly "unusual" transaction amount here — we just
picked the top 0.1% largest ones (1,000 transactions), but they aren't actually
suspicious, just naturally the highest numbers in a random range.

**Why it matters:** In a real fraud-detection system, you wouldn't compare one
transaction to *everyone's* spending — you'd compare it to *that specific customer's*
usual spending pattern. If someone who normally spends $50 suddenly spends $5,000,
that's suspicious, even though $5,000 isn't a large transaction overall. This dataset
doesn't have the kind of realistic spending patterns needed to demonstrate that kind
of detection, but it's an important distinction to understand and explain.

---

## The Big Picture

If someone asks you "what did you learn from this project," here's the honest,
interview-ready answer:

> "I analyzed a synthetic banking dataset covering customers, accounts, loans, and a
> million transactions. The data was extremely clean, so I focused on testing whether
> it behaved the way real banking data should. I found that several relationships you'd
> expect in real data — like credit score affecting interest rates, or transaction
> amounts clustering around typical spending — simply weren't there, which told me the
> data was randomly generated rather than modeled on real customer behavior. I built a
> customer risk segmentation and a transaction-flagging method that are both
> methodologically sound and would work well on real data, but I was careful to call out
> that the specific thresholds would need to be recalibrated against a real population
> before being trusted in production."

That's a more valuable takeaway than "the numbers were X" — it shows judgment, not just
execution.
